title: Warfarin, infection and bruising
brief: HMR referral: Mara, 76, lives independently and wants to keep managing her own medicines. She has atrial fibrillation, hypertension and osteoarthritis.
She bought aspirin 300 mg tablets and has taken two most days this week for knee pain. She started amoxicillin/clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily for a chest infection three days ago.
She reports new bruises and one episode of blood when brushing her teeth. Her last documented INR was 2.4 two weeks ago.
actor: If asked, Mara says she took aspirin most days this week because it worked better than paracetamol.
She has not told the INR clinic about the antibiotic. The dispensing label confirms amoxicillin/clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily; no other new medicines.
She has no black stools, severe headache, fall or persistent bleeding today, but the bruising is new.
key: Major: New bruising and gum bleeding while taking warfarin plus self-selected aspirin 600 mg on most days. Aspirin adds antiplatelet and gastrointestinal bleeding risk even if INR is in range; the INR of 2.4 predates both changes.
Moderate: Amoxicillin/clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily and acute infection may destabilise anticoagulation; the INR clinic has not been informed.
Minor: Knee osteoarthritis pain is not controlled with the current paracetamol 500–1000 mg as needed; the patient chose aspirin without checking interactions.

Assess bleeding now (amount, persistence, melaena, haematuria, headache, falls, dizziness). Arrange same-day GP/INR-clinic advice and repeat INR promptly; urgent emergency assessment for significant or ongoing bleeding, head injury or neurological symptoms.

Advise no further aspirin for knee pain unless a clinician confirms a separate cardiovascular indication. Do not independently change warfarin dose; send the antibiotic name, aspirin exposure, symptoms and last INR to the INR service.
Review what paracetamol dose/frequency Mara has actually used and discuss a safer pain plan, activity support and GP review if pain persists.

Confirm INR result and clinic-directed warfarin plan today; repeat as directed during and after the antibiotic course. Recheck bleeding within 24–48 hours and ensure Mara knows who to call. Document the reconciled list and handoff.

title: Diabetes, CKD and a recent illness
brief: HMR referral: Ravi, 69, has type 2 diabetes, CKD and hypertension. He lives with his partner and would prefer a simple regimen.
He has had vomiting and poor oral intake for 48 hours but continued his regular medicines. He reports two morning episodes of shakiness relieved by juice.
Recent eGFR was 38 mL/min/1.73 m²; HbA1c 7.1%.
actor: If asked, Ravi checked one shaky episode yesterday: capillary glucose was 3.3 mmol/L before juice; he has no ketone meter.
He has passed less urine today and feels light-headed on standing.
He is worried that stopping any medicine, even briefly, will harm him.
key: Major: Glucose 3.3 mmol/L with symptoms while taking gliclazide MR 60 mg daily and eating poorly: recurrent hypoglycaemia risk.

Major: Vomiting, reduced urine and postural light-headedness while continuing empagliflozin 10 mg, metformin 1 g twice daily and irbesartan 150 mg: dehydration, acute kidney injury and SGLT2-associated ketoacidosis risk; eGFR 38 is a month old.
Moderate: Metformin 2 g/day needs renal-dose and tolerance review at eGFR 38; a current renal result is needed before a long-term decision.
Minor: No written sick-day plan despite diabetes, CKD and multiple medicines that need review during illness.

Arrange same-day clinical assessment: capillary glucose now, hydration, ketones if indicated, current creatinine/eGFR, electrolytes and acid-base assessment if unwell. Treat current hypoglycaemia according to local protocol and confirm a repeat glucose.

Discuss a temporary sick-day hold of empagliflozin, metformin and irbesartan during significant vomiting/dehydration with the treating clinician; gliclazide MR needs urgent review while intake is poor and low glucose has occurred. Do not leave Ravi to restart medicines by guesswork.
After recovery, ask the GP/diabetes team to review metformin dose against current renal function and whether gliclazide MR 60 mg remains appropriate given hypoglycaemia and HbA1c 7.1%.

Document which medicine is held, who authorises/restarts it, glucose monitoring frequency, fluids and food intake, and repeat renal function/electrolytes. Review within 24 hours while ill; restart only when eating/drinking normally and renal status is acceptable per clinician plan. Escalate for persistent vomiting, ketones, confusion or inability to keep fluids down.

title: Heart failure, blood pressure and ibuprofen
brief: HMR referral: Elaine, 73, has heart failure, hypertension and chronic back pain. She has new ankle swelling and has needed two pillows at night this week.
She sometimes skips her diuretic on days out because of toilet access. She bought ibuprofen for back pain this week.
Home BP readings average 156/88 mmHg; her weight is 2.5 kg above her usual value.
actor: If asked, she is more breathless walking to the letterbox but is comfortable at rest.
She bought ibuprofen because she did not realise it could affect her heart or kidneys.
She wants help finding a pain option that lets her stay active.
key: Major: Possible decompensated heart failure: new orthopnoea, ankle oedema, 2.5 kg weight gain and exertional breathlessness.
Moderate: Ibuprofen 400 mg up to three times daily for a week can worsen fluid retention, BP and renal function in heart failure, especially with perindopril 5 mg and furosemide 40 mg.
Moderate: Furosemide 40 mg morning doses are skipped on days out; this may contribute to fluid overload.
Minor: Home BP averaging 156/88 mmHg and back pain need review after the acute congestion is addressed.
Arrange same-day GP/heart-failure assessment for volume status and diuretic plan; emergency assessment if breathless at rest, chest pain, syncope or severe hypoxia.
Ask Elaine to stop self-selected ibuprofen and confirm no other NSAID. Discuss a clinician-approved alternative pain plan and non-drug back-pain strategies.
Do not independently increase furosemide. Explore timed dosing, toilet access and a written action plan with GP/cardiology so outings do not mean missed doses.

Check current creatinine/eGFR, potassium, sodium, pulse, BP, oxygenation if available, weight trend and oedema. Daily morning weight and symptom diary; GP reviews treatment response within 24–48 hours and labs after any diuretic/ACE inhibitor adjustment.

title: Thyroid replacement and administration
brief: HMR referral: Zoe, 58, has hypothyroidism, iron-deficiency anaemia and reflux. She reports fatigue. Her TSH was 9.8 mIU/L (local range 0.4–4.0) last week.
She takes all tablets together with breakfast to avoid forgetting them.
The GP referral asks for review of her thyroid treatment.
actor: If asked, Zoe has used the same levothyroxine dose for years but started iron six weeks ago.
She sometimes misses weekend doses and is concerned about a complicated schedule.
She has no severe acute symptoms.
key: Major: Levothyroxine 100 micrograms is taken with breakfast and ferrous sulfate 325 mg, and sometimes calcium carbonate 600 mg. Iron/calcium reduce absorption; TSH 9.8 mIU/L is above the local range.
Moderate: Missed weekend levothyroxine doses make the apparent treatment failure harder to interpret; raising the dose first could overshoot once administration improves.
Moderate: Iron-deficiency anaemia remains a plausible separate cause of fatigue: Hb 108 g/L and ferritin 12 micrograms/L were low six weeks ago.
Minor: Pantoprazole 40 mg may add to absorption complexity; confirm need, duration and administration rather than stopping it abruptly.

Keep the prescribed levothyroxine dose initially and agree a consistent fasting schedule: 100 micrograms with water 30–60 minutes before breakfast; separate iron and calcium by at least four hours. If mornings are unworkable, discuss a consistent bedtime empty-stomach schedule with the GP.

Move ferrous sulfate 325 mg to a later time that Zoe can reliably follow. Use a simple written timetable and weekend reminder. Do not recommend a new thyroxine dose based on one result while administration is inconsistent.
Ask GP to review anaemia cause and response to iron and whether pantoprazole 40 mg remains indicated.

Repeat TSH (and free T4 if GP requests) about 6 weeks after stable administration; review fatigue, adherence, Hb/ferritin and iron tolerance. GP adjusts levothyroxine only after trend and actual use are clear.

title: Depression, sleep and falls
brief: HMR referral: Nola, 79, reports low mood and poor sleep after a bereavement. She has fallen twice in three months and is afraid of losing independence.
She says her antidepressant has not helped, but the start date and adherence are unclear. Diazepam is used most nights.
Her daughter fills a weekly medicine organiser.
actor: If asked, Nola sometimes feels dizzy when rising and is sleepy in the morning.
She takes diazepam because she fears a sleepless night and does not want it stopped abruptly.
She denies immediate self-harm intent but says some days feel hopeless; a fuller risk assessment is needed.
key: Major: Two falls with morning sedation and postural dizziness while taking diazepam 5 mg most nights, oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily and intermittent paracetamol/codeine. Cumulative sedative and anticholinergic load threatens safety.
Major: Low mood and hopelessness need a direct suicide/self-harm and functioning assessment; current denial of immediate intent does not complete the assessment.
Moderate: Sertraline 50 mg efficacy cannot be judged until start date, regular use, duration, response and adverse effects are known.
Minor: Possible orthostatic contribution from amlodipine 5 mg; a seated BP of 128/72 two weeks ago does not rule out standing hypotension.
Assess immediate injury and mental-health safety today; arrange urgent mental-health assessment if intent, plan or inability to stay safe emerges.

With Nola and GP, prioritise a gradual diazepam taper from the actual nightly 5 mg use; do not stop abruptly. Review whether oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily still helps and whether a lower-anticholinergic bladder approach is possible; verify exact paracetamol/codeine product and use.
Check sertraline duration/adherence and ask GP to reassess depression, grief and sleep after adequate trial; discuss psychological support and falls-prevention/physiotherapy.

Check lying/standing BP, falls diary, alertness, cognition, sleep, mood and urinary symptoms. GP/pharmacist review within 1–2 weeks and at each taper step; involve daughter with consent and confirm medicine organiser matches the plan.

title: Asthma control and inhaler use
brief: HMR referral: James, 34, has asthma and allergic rhinitis. He has used a reliever on most days this month and wakes coughing twice a week.
His preventer refills have been irregular. He has no written asthma action plan.
He recently changed jobs and is exposed to dust.
actor: If asked, James avoids the preventer because he dislikes its taste and is unsure whether it is needed when he feels well.
He can speak comfortably now and has no current severe breathlessness.
He wants a plan that fits a rotating shift schedule.
key: Major: Poor asthma control: salbutamol needed most days and night waking twice weekly; risk of future exacerbation.
Moderate: Budesonide/formoterol 200/6 prescribed one inhalation twice daily has irregular refills; the preventer is often skipped because of taste and uncertainty about need.
Moderate: No written action plan; new dust exposure and intermittent fluticasone nasal spray use may contribute to uncontrolled airways symptoms.
Assess current severity now: speech, work of breathing, reliever response, peak flow if available; urgent care for severe breathlessness or poor response.

Observe inhaler technique with the exact device; check remaining doses, adherence and mouth-rinsing. Explain purpose of the prescribed budesonide/formoterol 200/6 regimen and develop reminders compatible with shifts. Do not increase it solely from refill history.
Arrange GP/asthma clinician review of control, regimen and written action plan; address workplace dust exposure and regular rhinitis treatment technique if indicated.

Track daytime symptoms, night waking, reliever use and peak flow if part of the action plan. Review technique/adherence within 1–2 weeks and reassess control after a consistent treatment trial; seek immediate help for inability to speak, cyanosis or worsening despite reliever.

title: Chronic pain with liver and renal risk
brief: HMR referral: Tomas, 67, has knee osteoarthritis, chronic liver disease, CKD and prior peptic ulcer disease. Pain is limiting his walks.

For three weeks he has taken paracetamol modified-release 665 mg, two tablets three times daily, plus Panadol 500 mg immediate-release, two tablets at bedtime. He also bought naproxen 250 mg and takes one tablet twice daily.
He drinks 2–3 glasses of wine on some weekends and has new right upper abdominal discomfort. The GP requests a pain and medicine safety review.
actor: If asked, the Panadol label reads paracetamol 500 mg per tablet and he takes two at bedtime as well as all six modified-release tablets.
He takes naproxen 250 mg with breakfast and dinner and values walking to the shops.
He has right upper abdominal discomfort but denies vomiting blood or black stools today; ask about jaundice, confusion, alcohol intake and total use.
key: Major: Total paracetamol is 4,990 mg/day: modified release 665 mg × 2 × 3 = 3,990 mg plus Panadol paracetamol 500 mg × 2 = 1,000 mg. This exceeds the usual adult 4 g/day maximum in a patient with liver disease, abdominal symptoms and ALT 132 U/L (ref 5–40).
Major: Naproxen 250 mg twice daily for 3 weeks with CKD (eGFR 44), prior ulcer and irbesartan 150 mg increases AKI and GI bleeding risk; Hb 118 g/L is below range.
Moderate: Knee pain remains function-limiting despite high-risk self-treatment; no function-based goal or non-drug plan.
Minor: Weekend alcohol and unrecognised paracetamol duplication increase the risk of repeat exposure.

Arrange same-day GP/urgent assessment for repeated supratherapeutic paracetamol use, abdominal discomfort and abnormal liver tests; call Poisons Information Centre 13 11 26 for case-specific advice if ongoing/uncertain exposure. Do not wait for symptoms to worsen.

Stop the additional Panadol immediate-release tablets and self-selected naproxen while obtaining clinical advice; record exact products, amounts and timing. The GP should decide a safe future paracetamol limit and analgesic plan in light of liver/renal disease.
Discuss knee exercise/physiotherapy, weight/load modification and pain/function goals; avoid a generic opioid substitution.

Same-day clinical review of liver panel, INR/synthetic function if ordered, renal function, blood count and bleeding symptoms; follow trend as directed. Confirm one written analgesic list and review pain/function within 1–2 weeks after a safer plan is agreed.

title: Discharge list and duplicate therapy
brief: HMR referral: Leila, 71, was discharged five days ago after an acute coronary syndrome. She has diabetes and hypertension and is confused by the new medicine list.
Her old weekly pack still contains medicines from before admission; she has been taking tablets from both the pack and new boxes.
She reports light-headedness.
actor: If asked, Leila has the discharge paperwork and all medicine boxes at home.
She has no current chest pain, shortness of breath or bleeding, but would need urgent assessment if these appear.
Her preferred pharmacy can repack the medicines once the list is confirmed.
key: Major: Leila is taking simvastatin 40 mg from the old pack plus discharge atorvastatin 80 mg nightly: unintended duplicate statin exposure and adverse-effect risk.

Major: Taking from both the old pack and new boxes after ACS creates possible omissions or duplicate doses of aspirin 100 mg, clopidogrel 75 mg and metoprolol MR 47.5 mg; exact intake must be verified today.
Moderate: Light-headedness may relate to continued amlodipine 10 mg plus new metoprolol; discharge BP 118/68 and pulse 64 are five days old.
Minor: Metformin 500 mg twice daily is on the pre-admission list but not confirmed on discharge; diabetes plan and pack need reconciliation.

Ask Leila to bring all boxes, old pack and discharge list today; obtain actual dose history and current BP/pulse. Contact discharge team/GP and community pharmacy for the intended signed list; do not infer that an omitted medicine should be stopped or restarted.

Hold use of the unverified old pack while a safe interim supply is arranged with the prescriber/pharmacy. Remove simvastatin from the new pack if the discharge regimen confirms atorvastatin 80 mg. Ensure aspirin 100 mg and clopidogrel 75 mg are not inadvertently missed; do not change antiplatelets without cardiology advice.
Create one dated list, repack only after confirmation, use teach-back and involve a supporter with Leila’s consent.

Same-day confirmation of what she actually took, BP/pulse and symptoms; urgent help for chest pain, syncope, severe bleeding or shortness of breath. Recheck new pack against the confirmed list and follow up in 24–48 hours; monitor muscle pain/dark urine, bleeding, BP and pulse.

title: A child's spreading skin lesions
brief: Sarah asks for treatment for yellow crusted sores around the mouth and nose of her son Hugo, 6 years old (22 kg). He is at school and she has a phone photo.
She wants to know whether she can obtain treatment here and whether Hugo can attend school tomorrow.
actor: Hugo has four small sores around the mouth/nose, beginning as blisters four days ago; a younger sibling now has one similar sore. The mother can show a photo.
No fever, lethargy, rapidly spreading redness or chronic illness. No regular medicines; children’s paracetamol was used for a recent cold. No known medicine allergy.

Moderate: Spread to a sibling and school contacts; assess each affected person and ARF risk rather than assuming ethnicity alone determines referral.

Invite Sarah to bring Hugo for assessment today; confirm photo findings with lesion count, age/weight, allergies, medicines, systemic symptoms, residence/ARF risk and coexisting skin disease. Refer if extensive, severe, ulcerating, recurrent, high ARF risk or uncertain diagnosis.
Explain gentle cleansing, hand hygiene, short nails, covering lesions where practical and avoiding shared towels. Assess the sibling and give current local school-exclusion advice.
Set a clear review after treatment starts; seek earlier care for fever, spreading redness, swelling, systemic illness or no improvement. Record treatment, family advice and referral pathway.

title: Shingles near the eye
brief: Daniel, 62, asks for aciclovir cream for a painful blistering rash on the right forehead that began yesterday.

title: Painful swimmer's ear
displayTitle: After a week at the pool
brief: Mia, 28, asks for ear drops for right ear pain after swimming every day this week. She has seen a little discharge.
Assess the presentation and decide whether a pharmacy treatment pathway is appropriate.
actor: Pain is worse when the outer ear is moved; there is mild itch and scant discharge.
No fever, severe pain, dizziness or facial weakness. No diabetes or immunosuppression. No known allergies; no regular medicines.
They used a cotton bud yesterday and are unsure whether the eardrum is intact.
key: Major: Otitis externa is plausible from pinna-movement pain, itch and discharge, but the tympanic membrane has not been examined; possible perforation changes scope and drop safety.
Moderate: Cotton-bud use and continued swimming may perpetuate canal trauma and moisture.

Take full history, examine ear canal and tympanic membrane with appropriate otoscopy if trained/equipped, assess hearing and red flags. If the membrane cannot be visualised or perforation is suspected, refer rather than selecting a potentially ototoxic drop.

If uncomplicated and eligible, use the Queensland otitis externa pathway and exact eTG/AMH regimen for the observed canal findings; do not use routine oral antibiotics. Explain drop administration and keeping the ear dry.

Expected improvement is usually within 48–72 hours; reassess or refer sooner for fever, spreading infection, severe pain, hearing change, dizziness or facial weakness. No improvement by 48–72 hours needs review.

title: Hay fever that is not controlled
brief: Olivia, 23, asks for a stronger hay-fever product. She takes loratadine 10 mg most mornings but still has daily sneezing and a blocked nose.
She drives for work and needs to remain alert. Assess and manage the request.
actor: Springtime sneezing, clear runny nose, nasal blockage and itchy eyes on most days; no fever, unilateral symptoms, facial pain or bleeding.

Loratadine 10 mg is taken most mornings. She tried fluticasone nasal spray 50 micrograms/spray, one spray in each nostril for only two days, then stopped. No other medicines, conditions or allergies; not pregnant.

key: Moderate: Persistent nasal obstruction despite loratadine 10 mg daily; the two-day fluticasone trial and poor technique are inadequate to judge intranasal steroid failure.
Minor: Driving makes sedating antihistamines an unattractive choice.

Check red flags and confirm allergic pattern, adherence and product technique. For the 50 micrograms/spray fluticasone propionate product she already owns, a usual adult starting regimen is 2 sprays in each nostril once daily (200 micrograms/day), then 1 spray each nostril daily when controlled; verify her product label and suitability. Discuss allergen avoidance and saline rinse if acceptable; an eye product may be considered if itchy eyes remain troublesome after nasal control.
Agree a review after 2–4 weeks of correct daily use; refer sooner for unilateral obstruction, bleeding, fever, severe facial pain or no response after an adequate trial.

title: Reflux with an alarm feature

title: Vomiting and reduced urine
brief: A parent asks for ondansetron for their 2-year-old child, Eva (12 kg), after repeated vomiting since yesterday.

title: Knee pain and an NSAID request

title: Contraception continuation request

brief: Amelia, 29, asks for continuation of her levonorgestrel 150 micrograms/ethinylestradiol 30 micrograms combined pill. Her GP appointment is in three weeks.

title: New antibiotic with warfarin
brief: You are the pharmacist. Evelyn, 74, presents a prescription from Dr M. Patel for clarithromycin 500 mg tablets: take one tablet every 12 hours for 7 days; quantity 14, no repeats. The prescription states “chest infection”.
The dispensing record shows warfarin with a variable dose managed by an INR clinic. Evelyn asks to collect the antibiotic quickly and leave.
Assess the prescription and the person, then explain and carry out a safe plan.
actor: If asked, Evelyn takes variable warfarin doses and has not had an INR for about three weeks. She has not yet told the INR clinic about this prescription.
She has a cough but no fever, severe breathlessness or chest pain. She noticed mild blood in her urine today; ask further about bleeding and escalation.
No known medicine allergies. Other regular medicines: perindopril 5 mg daily and atorvastatin 20 mg nightly; no other antibiotics.
key: Major: Visible haematuria today while taking warfarin with no INR for about three weeks requires same-day medical assessment for bleeding and cause, before routine antibiotic supply.
Major: Clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily for 7 days can increase warfarin effect and interacts with atorvastatin 20 mg; the prescriber and INR service need a coordinated alternative/monitoring plan.

Request an appropriate alternative antibiotic based on diagnosis/allergy and arrange INR-clinic instructions.

title: Eczema flare or infection?
brief: Clara, 32, has known atopic dermatitis. She asks for a stronger steroid because a forearm patch is now red, weepy and sore despite hydrocortisone 1% cream.
Assess whether this is a flare, infection or another condition before choosing treatment.
actor: The 4 cm patch is more painful than usual and has honey-coloured crusting. No fever, rapidly spreading redness or other lesions.
She uses hydrocortisone 1% twice daily for two days of each flare and an emollient only when itchy. No other medicines or known allergies.
She has a family event soon and wants rapid improvement; she can return for assessment if needed.
key: Major: Pain, weeping and honey-coloured crusting raise secondary bacterial infection/impetiginised eczema; increasing steroid potency alone misses the possible infection.
Moderate: Intermittent emollient use and brief hydrocortisone 1% courses may contribute to poor eczema control; distinguish technique/adherence from treatment failure.

Examine extent, warmth, spreading erythema, fever and other sites; assess Queensland impetigo/atopic dermatitis eligibility. Treat or refer the infection component using the current pathway before deciding steroid strength; no blind escalation.
Explain regular fragrance-free emollient use, short appropriate anti-inflammatory course on eczema skin per product/guideline, gentle cleansing and infection-spread precautions.
Review within 48–72 hours or sooner for spreading erythema, fever, systemic symptoms or worsening pain. Document lesion appearance and chosen pathway.

title: Psoriasis flare on sensitive sites
brief: Min, 46, has plaque psoriasis on the elbows and asks to reuse betamethasone dipropionate 0.05% ointment on a new face and groin rash.
Conduct a private consultation and decide what advice or referral is needed.
actor: The facial/groin rash is new and has never been diagnosed. They also have new morning swelling and pain in two fingers lasting about an hour.
No fever. Betamethasone dipropionate 0.05% is used on elbow plaques intermittently; no other regular medicines or known allergies.
They are embarrassed and prefer a discreet plan.
key: Major: New swollen painful fingers with morning stiffness may indicate psoriatic arthritis and warrant medical assessment to prevent joint damage.
Moderate: New face/groin rash is not confirmed psoriasis; potent betamethasone dipropionate 0.05% used on elbows is unsuitable for routine use on thin skin there without assessment.
Offer privacy; ask about joint pattern, function, extent, systemic symptoms and alternative rash causes. Arrange GP/dermatology and joint assessment, with urgency based on severity.
Advise against applying the strong elbow steroid to face/groin. Provide gentle skin care/emollient advice while awaiting a site-specific diagnosis and treatment plan.
Check that referral is booked and review symptoms; urgent care for a hot acutely swollen joint, fever or rapidly worsening widespread rash.

title: Smoking cessation with a treatment preference
brief: Noah, 41, wants to stop smoking before surgery in eight weeks. He asks whether a 21 mg nicotine patch might help.
Run a 10-minute patient-centred consultation and agree a practical first step.
actor: He smokes about 15 cigarettes daily; first cigarette is within 30 minutes of waking. One earlier quit attempt ended during a stressful week.
He takes sertraline 50 mg daily, has no known allergies, is not pregnant and wants an affordable plan. His partner smokes but is willing to help.
He is open to a quit date next week and combined patch plus short-acting nicotine product if explained.
key: Moderate: Daily smoking with first cigarette within 30 minutes indicates nicotine dependence; surgery in eight weeks makes timely cessation support valuable.
Minor: Prior stress-triggered relapse, partner smoking and cost could undermine adherence unless included in the plan.

Ask about dependence, withdrawal, prior method, triggers, mental health, other medicines, budget and preferred quit date. Discuss behavioural support plus NRT: a 21 mg daily patch is a plausible starting option for this level of dependence, with a short-acting form for breakthrough cravings after checking exact product directions and suitability in AMH/Queensland guidance.
Offer Quitline and a written quit date/trigger plan; ask the partner to support a smoke-free home. Review interactions with smoking cessation and any relevant medicines with the prescriber.

Review in the first week after quit date for cravings, adverse effects and patch use, then again before surgery; adjust NRT with the pharmacist/prescriber if cravings persist. Treat a lapse as information for the next attempt.

title: Lost opioid dose, distressed patient
brief: Tariq says his prescribed methadone 40 mg take-away dose for today was lost on the bus. He asks you to replace it immediately and is raising his voice.
Respond as the pharmacist, focusing on communication, safety and professional responsibilities.
actor: The patient is worried about withdrawal and missing work. They calm somewhat if you acknowledge this and speak privately.

The pharmacy record shows a methadone 40 mg take-away dose was supplied yesterday for today; there is no authority for a replacement. Tariq says the closed bottle was lost on the bus. He has no current severe withdrawal or intoxication signs.
They resist being told to 'just call tomorrow' but will accept a concrete plan for today.
key: Major: Replacement of a reported lost methadone 40 mg take-away dose cannot be promised or supplied without checking program authority, records and legal requirements; duplicate dosing could be dangerous.
Moderate: Tariq is distressed about withdrawal and work and needs a concrete same-day pathway.

Acknowledge the stress, offer a private safe space and ask about current symptoms/intoxication. State that you will check the record and contact the authorised prescriber/OTP service now; do not accuse him or promise a dose.
If the service cannot be reached, identify an urgent clinical assessment pathway for withdrawal/safety needs and arrange a call-back time. Document facts, contacts, advice and the agreed plan.
Check immediate safety before he leaves and confirm who will contact him today; escalate if intoxication, severe withdrawal or other acute risk develops.

title: Parent angry about no antibiotic
brief: A parent of a 5-year-old says, “The last pharmacist gave my child amoxicillin. Why won’t you? You’re wasting my time.” The child has two days of cough and runny nose.
Respond to the parent as the pharmacist. Focus on challenging communication and professional judgement.
actor: The parent is worried because the child missed school and they have missed work.
They will describe symptoms if asked calmly. They have not been given a clear reason why antibiotics may be unsuitable.
They are willing to consider a safety-net plan if they feel heard.
key: Moderate: The parent feels dismissed and needs a clear assessment and plan; a prior antibiotic supply is not evidence that this illness needs antibiotics.
Acknowledge missed school/work and ask what worries them most. Briefly assess fever, breathing, hydration, duration and red flags; offer clinician review if unwell.

Explain in plain language why antibiotics may not help an uncomplicated viral cold, without criticising the prior pharmacist. Agree practical symptom care, return criteria and access to assessment if needed.
Confirm understanding and a time to seek care if worse or not improving; urgent care for breathing difficulty, dehydration or marked lethargy.

title: Family member asks for private results
brief: A patient’s adult daughter asks what new antidepressant her father collected yesterday and why. He is not present and no consent is recorded. She says she manages his medicines and is offended when you hesitate.
Respond as the pharmacist.
actor: The daughter is genuinely worried and says he has become forgetful.
No consent or legal authority to share his record is documented. The patient is not present.
She is open to asking him to join a conversation if the offer is respectful.
key: Major: Disclosing the named antidepressant or indication without consent/authority would breach confidentiality.
Moderate: The daughter reports forgetfulness, which may warrant a supported safety review without unnecessary disclosure.
Acknowledge her care for him; explain you need his permission before discussing his record. Do not confirm or deny the medicine or indication.

Offer to call the patient with her present, arrange a three-way conversation after consent, or discuss general medicine-support options. If she reports immediate danger, use an appropriate urgent safety pathway and disclose only what is necessary under applicable rules.
Document the request, any consent obtained, and the agreed safe follow-up.

title: Dispensing error disclosed
brief: Priya returns with a box of amlodipine 10 mg. Her prescription and bag label say amlodipine 5 mg daily. She took one 10 mg tablet last night and asks if she has been harmed.
Respond as the pharmacist.
actor: She has no current symptoms but is frightened. The original prescription and supply record need checking; she has not taken a second dose.
She wants the pharmacy to acknowledge the mistake and explain what will happen next.
key: Major: Potential dispensing error: 10 mg amlodipine supplied against a 5 mg prescription and one double-strength dose taken; assess hypotension, dizziness, falls and other patient factors now.
Moderate: Priya needs honest disclosure, corrected supply and a clear follow-up owner.

Apologise and take the concern seriously. Verify prescription, product, label, batch and amount taken; check symptoms and BP if available, and seek prescriber/poisons advice if clinically indicated. Do not guess that one dose is harmless.
Secure the incorrect product, provide the correct 5 mg supply once verified, explain next-dose advice from the clinician, document the incident and tell Priya who will contact her.
Check for dizziness, fainting or falls today and follow up within 24 hours; urgent assessment for syncope, severe weakness or other concerning symptoms. Record the incident and preventive review.

title: Prescriber challenges your concern
brief: You phone Dr Chen about a new clarithromycin 500 mg twice-daily prescription for a patient who takes simvastatin 40 mg nightly. Dr Chen says, “I’ve prescribed this for years. Just dispense it.”
Respond to the prescriber while maintaining a professional working relationship.
actor: The prescriber is rushed and has not heard about the patient’s simvastatin 40 mg nightly.
They will consider an alternative antibiotic or explicit statin plan when the risk is stated clearly; the infection diagnosis and allergy history still need confirmation.
key: Major: Clarithromycin with simvastatin 40 mg is a serious interaction with myopathy/rhabdomyolysis risk; an unresolved concern should not be bypassed.
Moderate: The prescriber needs a short, patient-specific recommendation that respects time pressure.

Use a concise ISBAR: identify patient and prescription, state simvastatin 40 mg nightly and the interaction, then request an antibiotic alternative based on diagnosis/allergy or a prescriber-authorised statin interruption and restart plan.

Repeat back the agreed action, who contacts the patient, and what will be documented. If the risk remains unresolved, do not silently dispense; escalate to senior clinical advice according to local process.
Document the prescriber discussion and confirm the patient receives the final antibiotic/statin instructions and knows to report muscle pain or dark urine.

title: Cost blocks the agreed plan
brief: A patient says the fluticasone nasal spray you recommended costs more than they can pay. They say previous pharmacists made them feel judged and are about to leave untreated.
Respond as the pharmacist and agree an affordable, safe next step.
actor: They can afford a lower-cost product but do not want to discuss finances at the counter. They want relief from daily allergic-rhinitis symptoms.
They will discuss options privately and appreciate a simple written plan; no red flags are volunteered.
key: Moderate: Cost and prior stigma threaten treatment access and trust; a clinically suitable alternative must be checked rather than assumed equivalent.
Offer privacy, acknowledge the cost issue without judgement and ask for a comfortable budget. Confirm symptoms, prior therapies and exact fluticasone product/price.

Compare lower-cost intranasal corticosteroid options or other appropriate pathways based on the patient’s symptom profile, actual prices and product directions; offer a written plan or referral if none is affordable today.
Ask the patient to repeat the agreed use and review symptom benefit after an adequate trial; confirm they can obtain the chosen product.

title: Patient refuses urgent referral
brief: You recommended urgent assessment because a patient reports black stools and light-headedness. They reply, “I’m not going to hospital. I had a terrible experience there.”
Respond to the refusal while keeping the patient safe and respected.
actor: They fear being dismissed and leaving their child without care. They can understand information and decide for themselves.
Black stools and light-headedness are ongoing; there is no confirmed explanation. They may accept a support person or different urgent care pathway.
key: Major: Black stools with light-headedness may indicate significant GI bleeding; urgent assessment remains necessary even if the patient declines the first proposed route.
Moderate: Past care experience and childcare are real barriers that need practical solutions.

Listen to what happened previously, explain the concern and urgency in plain language, and check understanding and decision-making capacity. Offer to call an ambulance/urgent service, involve a support person and help solve childcare/transport.
If refusal persists, respect the decision, give explicit emergency triggers and document the discussion and offered options; do not falsely reassure or coerce.
Seek a concrete plan for where and when they will be assessed and who can check on them; escalate if collapse, worsening dizziness, ongoing bleeding or inability to stay safe.

title: Colleague bypasses an allergy alert
brief: A colleague asks you to hand over amoxicillin 500 mg capsules despite a penicillin allergy alert, saying it was “probably just nausea.” The patient is waiting and the queue is growing.
Respond to the colleague and protect the patient.
actor: The actual reaction has not been checked. If the patient is asked, they describe wheeze and facial swelling within an hour of amoxicillin several years ago.
The colleague is stressed rather than hostile and will accept a quick joint check.
key: Major: The patient’s reported wheeze and facial swelling after amoxicillin are compatible with immediate serious allergy; amoxicillin 500 mg must not be handed over without prescriber review.
Minor: Queue pressure and the colleague’s assumption create a process risk.
Say calmly, “Let’s pause this supply until we check the reaction.” Ask the patient what happened, timing and any treatment; verify record and contact prescriber for a suitable alternative.
Explain a brief safety delay to the patient without blaming the colleague. Update allergy record and document the new prescription/communication.
Confirm the patient received the alternative and understands the allergy record; escalate urgently if any dose was already taken and symptoms develop.
